# Systematic morphological and morphometric analysis of identified olfactory receptor neurons in Drosophila melanogaster ## Authors - Cesar Nava Gonzales1 - Quintyn McKaughan1 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-6611-6530](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6611-6530)) - Eric A Bushong2 - Kalyani Cauwenberghs1 - Renny Ng1 - Matthew Madany2 - Mark H Ellisman2 - Chih-Ying Su1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-0005-1890](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0005-1890)) † ### Affiliations 1. Neurobiology Section, Division of Biological Sciences, University of California, San Diego San Diego United States 2. National Center for Microscopy and Imaging Research, Center for Research in Biological Systems, University of California, San Diego San Diego United States † Corresponding author ## Abstract The biophysical properties of sensory neurons are influenced by their morphometric and morphological features, whose precise measurements require high-quality volume electron microscopy (EM). However, systematic surveys of nanoscale characteristics for identified neurons are scarce. Here, we characterize the morphology of Drosophila olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) across the majority of genetically identified sensory hairs. By analyzing serial block-face electron microscopy images of cryofixed antennal tissues, we compile an extensive morphometric data set based on 122 reconstructed 3D models for 33 of the 40 identified antennal ORN types. Additionally, we observe multiple novel features—including extracellular vacuoles within sensillum lumen, intricate dendritic branching, mitochondria enrichment in select ORNs, novel sensillum types, and empty sensilla containing no neurons—which raise new questions pertinent to cell biology and sensory neurobiology. Our systematic survey is critical for future investigations into how the size and shape of sensory neurons influence their responses, sensitivity, and circuit function. ## Introduction Most insect species, including agricultural pests and disease vectors, rely on olfaction to guide critical behaviors including foraging, feeding, mating, egg-laying, and aggression (Kim et al., 2017). Odor detection begins with the olfactory organs, the antenna and maxillary palp, which are covered with sensory hairs, or sensilla, that encapsulate the dendrites of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs). In Drosophila melanogaster, olfactory sensilla fall into four morphological classes—basiconic, coeloconic, intermediate, and trichoid—which are distinguished by their length, size, shape, and cuticular pore arrangement (Shanbhag et al., 1999). Notably, ORNs housed in different sensillum classes have distinct dendritic branching patterns and odor tuning properties. The outer dendritic segments of basiconic and intermediate ORNs display multiple branches, whereas the outer dendrites of coeloconic and trichoid neurons are typically unbranched (Shanbhag et al., 1999). While basiconic ORNs respond to a wide range of odorants, trichoid neurons respond predominantly to pheromones, and most coeloconic neurons are selectively tuned to amines and carboxylic acids (Dweck et al., 2015; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Lin et al., 2016; Silbering et al., 2011; van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007; Yao et al., 2005). The link between sensillum class, dendritic branching pattern, and odor tuning property suggests that the morphological features of sensilla and ORNs likely influence olfactory function. However, testing this possibility requires a systematic survey of these morphological features at nanoscales for neurons whose receptors have been identified and whose odor response profiles have been characterized. The majority of antennal sensilla house multiple ORNs. Each neuron is assigned a designation indicating the host sensillum and its relative extracellular spike amplitude among grouped neurons. Typically two and up to four ORNs are compartmentalized in a sensillum in stereotyped combinations—whereby a neuron expressing a particular receptor is always paired with a neighboring neuron that expresses another specific receptor (Benton et al., 2009; Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Hallem et al., 2004). For example, the Or59b receptor is expressed in the ab2A neuron, which is located in the antennal basiconic sensillum of type 2, while the ‘A’ indicates that its spike amplitude is greater than that of the neighboring ab2B neuron, which invariably expresses the Or85a receptor (Hallem et al., 2004). Interestingly, deleting or substituting the tuning receptor for an ORN does not alter its characteristic spike amplitude (Dobritsa, van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007; Hallem et al., 2004), suggesting that spike amplitude is a feature independent of receptor identity. The genetically predetermined pairing of neurons implies functional significance for this arrangement. Indeed, ORNs housed in the same sensillum can inhibit each other by means of direct electrical interaction, termed ephaptic coupling, which can also modulate fruitfly behavior in response to odor mixtures (Su et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2019). Strikingly, in most sensillum types, lateral inhibition is asymmetric between compartmentalized ORNs: the large-spike neuron is not only capable of exerting greater ephaptic influence but is also less susceptible to ephaptic inhibition by its small-spike neighbors. Mechanistically, this functional disparity arises from the size difference between grouped neurons. The large-spike ORN has a larger soma than its small-spike neighbor(s); this feature is translated into a smaller input resistance for the ‘A’ neuron, thus accounting for its dominance in ephaptic interaction (Zhang et al., 2019). These findings indicate a causal relationship between an ORN’s morphometric features and its circuit function. Taken together, these observations highlight the necessity and value of a systematic morphometric survey of genetically identified ORNs. Pioneering transmission electron microscopy (TEM) studies of high-pressure frozen and freeze-substituted (i.e., cryofixed) antennal tissues have provided a high-quality morphological atlas of Drosophila ORNs (Shanbhag et al., 1999; Shanbhag et al., 2000). However, for morphometric analysis, the utility of this atlas is limited because the 3D structure and molecular identity of ORNs are undefined. Taking advantage of the CryoChem method, which we have previously developed to permit high-quality ultrastructural preservation of cryofixed and genetically labeled samples for volume EM (Tsang et al., 2018), we have acquired serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBEM) images of antennal tissues in which select ORNs expressed a membrane-tethered EM marker (APEX2-mCD8GFP or APEX2-ORCO) (Tsang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019). In a previous study, we focused our analysis on the soma of labeled ORNs and their co-compartmentalized neuronal partners in five sensillum types (Zhang et al., 2019). Yet, in addition to the APEX2-labeled hairs, each SBEM data set contains many other sensilla, whose identity can be determined by cross-referencing the sensillum morphology and the number of its compartmentalized ORNs (Benton et al., 2009; Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Grabe et al., 2016; Lin and Potter, 2015; Shanbhag et al., 1999, Shanbhag et al., 2000). For example, among the three large basiconic sensillum types, ab1 can be identified without genetic labeling because the sensillum houses four neurons, whereas ab2 and ab3 both house two ORNs. Moreover, within a known sensillum, the ‘A’ or ‘B’ ORN can be distinguished according to the soma size. That is, the spike amplitude ratio between grouped neurons reflects their soma size differential (Zhang et al., 2019). Here, we conduct a systematic morphological and morphometric analysis of identified Drosophila ORNs. By segmenting SBEM images, we reconstruct 3D structures for neurons housed in 13 of the 19 genetically defined antennal sensillum types (Benton et al., 2009; Lin and Potter, 2015), covering all four morphological classes: the basiconic (ab1–5), coeloconic (ac1–4), intermediate (ai2 and ai3), and trichoid sensilla (at1 and at4) from a total of 158 reconstructed 3D sensillum models. Furthermore, based on 122 reconstructed 3D ORN models, we perform morphometric analysis for 33 of the 40 identified antennal ORN types (Task and Lin, 2021), as well as for 4 novel neuronal types. Our high-resolution survey uncovers multiple novel features, including extracellular vacuoles in the sensillum lumen, mitochondria-enriched inner dendritic enlargement, empty sensilla which house no ORNs, and two hitherto uncharacterized basiconic sensillum types. We also show that the outer dendritic branching pattern is much more intricate than previously appreciated. The information provided here defines new questions about how the size and shape of sensory neurons influence their responses, sensitivity, and circuit function, and sets the stage for future investigations into the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying diverse ORN morphologies. ## Results and discussion We began with a detailed survey of the SBEM images we had previously generated using female antennal tissues (Zhang et al., 2019). Individual data sets, acquired from different flies and named on the basis of the APEX2-expressing ORNs, included numerous sensory hairs in addition to the sensilla that housed labeled neurons (Figure 1A). In agreement with the characteristic topographical distribution of sensilla on the antenna (de Bruyne et al., 2001; Grabe et al., 2016; Shanbhag et al., 1999), the four morphological sensillum classes were unevenly represented in our eight SBEM data sets (Figure 1B,C). A total of 541 sensilla were sampled from these data sets, comparable to the total number of sensilla on an antenna (Shanbhag et al., 1999). Among the whole sensilla which were sampled in their entirety, we identified 37 basiconic, 30 coeloconic, 40 intermediate, and 51 trichoid sensilla based on their distinctive morphological features (Shanbhag et al., 1999). Briefly, the cuticle of basiconic, intermediate, and trichoid sensilla is decorated with numerous pores which serve as passages for odorants. The pores of basiconic sensilla are arranged in characteristic arrays, whereas those of trichoid and intermediate sensilla appear to scatter irregularly on the cuticular surface. The trichoid and intermediate sensilla are further recognized by their cylindrical, thickened bases, termed the ‘basal drum’ (Figure 1D). In contrast, the cuticle of the coeloconic sensilla does not contain any pores but instead consists of multiple cuticular fingers (Figure 1D), between which numerous spoke channels allow odorants access to ORNs (Shanbhag et al., 1999). ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/69896/elife-69896-fig1-v2.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) SBEM data sets analyzed in this study, named according to the genetically labeled ORNs (lower left corner, the receptor, and ORN identity are indicated). For the completely sampled sensilla, we reconstructed their 3D models and performed morphometric analysis. Within a morphological class, sensillum identity was determined by the number of enclosed neurons and by genetic labeling when this information was available. Of note, the distribution of individual sensillum types on the antenna follows a characteristic topographical pattern (de Bruyne et al., 2001; Grabe et al., 2016; Shanbhag et al., 1999). Therefore, for an unlabeled sensillum, its proximity to the labeled sensillum type may further aid its identification (see Large basiconic sensillum section below). For basiconic sensilla, we identified all three large basiconic sensilla (ab1, ab2, and ab3), one thin basiconic (ab4), and one small basiconic sensillum (ab5). Unexpectedly, we also found two novel types of basiconic sensilla: one large basiconic housing three neurons, which we termed abx(3), and the other, a small basiconic housing only one neuron, which we termed abx(1). For the other three morphological sensillum classes, all of the reported subtypes were identified, including four coeloconic, two intermediate, and three trichoid sensilla (Figure 1D). We further measured the length, surface area, cuticular, and lumen volumes of these identified sensilla (Table 1). The coeloconic sensilla are the shortest (5–8 μm), followed by the ab5 small basiconic (8–10 μm). The intermediate, thin, and large basiconic sensilla are of similar length (10–14 μm), while the trichoid sensilla are the longest (19–24 μm) (Figure 1E). In the remainder of this article, we focus on individual sensillum types, describe their identification, and provide morphological and morphometric information for their neurons (see Source data files for detailed information). ### Trichoid sensilla #### T1 sensillum Distinctly among trichoids, the T1 sensillum houses only a single neuron expressing the Or67d receptor that responds to the male fly pheromone, cVA (Couto et al., 2005; Kurtovic et al., 2007; Shanbhag et al., 1999; Ha and Smith, 2006; van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007). The ORN soma is located approximately 8–16 μm beneath the antennal surface (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with an average size of 47 μm3 (Table 2). The dendrite is divided into the inner and outer segments by the ciliary constriction (Figure 2A; Shanbhag et al., 1999). Situated entirely beneath the antennal surface, the inner dendritic segment is ensheathed by the thecogen cell, which is itself enveloped by the trichogen processes and then further surrounded by the tormogen cell (Figures 2A–7 and 8). The inner dendrite exhibits a wider diameter (0.75–1.5 μm) than the outer dendrite (~0.3 μm), which extends into the sensillum lumen with a slight taper (Figure 2A) or with a markedly flattened distal segment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Video 1). Although the T1 outer dendrite is believed to be typically unbranched (Shanbhag et al., 1999), we observed that among the four segmented T1 ORNs, one exhibits three branches and another six (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C and Video 1). In both cases, the dendrites began branching approximately halfway through the dendritic length inside the lumen, with secondary branching occurring further along distally (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C). Besides the dendritic branches, we observed free, extracellular membrane-bound structures within the lumen in 4 of the 19 analyzed T1 sensilla (21%) (see Table 1—source data 1 for details). These membranous structures, which we referred to as vacuoles, were predominantly found in the proximal region of the sensillum (Figure 2A-4-6). They vary considerably in size (0.2–2.0 μm in diameter) and do not appear to have a regular shape (Figure 2A). In some cases, the vacuole occupied nearly an entire segment of the lumen, reducing the ORN dendrite to the margin (Figures 2A–4). Although their functional significance remains to be determined, the extracellular vacuoles are likely derived from the tormogen auxiliary cell. In one T1 sensillum, we found that its tormogen cell extended a bulbous protrusion into the lumen, resembling the process of membrane budding (Figure 2B). Immediately adjacent to the bulbous protrusion was a small vacuole (Figure 2B). The close proximity between these two structures suggests that the free vacuoles within the lumen may have originated from the tormogen cell. #### T2 and T3 sensilla In addition to T1, we identified the other two trichoid sensillum types—T2 and T3—containing two and three neurons, respectively (Shanbhag et al., 1999; Figure 1). All trichoid sensilla are similar in length (19–24 μm), but T1 is distinctively narrower than T2 or T3 with smaller sensillum surface area and volume (Figure 1C,D and Table 1). In contrast, T2 and T3 cannot be distinguished externally from their morphological or morphometric features (Figure 1C,D and Table 1). In addition to providing nanoscale measurements of 33 identified ORN types and their corresponding sensillum apparatus, our analysis reveals several novel features of olfactory sensilla, including extracellular vacuoles, empty sensilla, and two previously uncharacterized basiconic sensillum types. Additionally, we find that not all at4 sensilla house three neurons; a subset contains only two ORNs. For most ORN types, neurons expressing the same receptor can display marked variability in their dendritic branching and morphology, suggesting that these features are not entirely genetically predetermined but are instead dynamically regulated. Moreover, contrary to the previously proposed paintbrush model, the basiconic outer dendrites exhibit a highly intricate branching pattern: diverging points are numerous, and branches can bifurcate or converge with others. Within basiconic sensilla, the large-spike ORNs selectively exhibit enlarged inner dendrites which are enriched with mitochondria. Furthermore, a remarkable morphological disparity is observed between compartmentalized ab2 neurons; the large-spike ‘A’ neuron sprouts more than 300 dendritic branches occupying nearly the entire sensillum lumen, whereas the neighboring ‘B’ neuron has only one unbranched outer dendrite. These observations raise many interesting questions. For example, what is the functional significance of the extracellular vacuoles commonly found in the basiconic lumen? Does the mitochondria-enriched inner dendritic enlargement influence olfactory response properties? What molecules regulate the diverse outer dendritic morphology? Does the surface area disparity between neighboring neurons (e.g., ab2A vs. ab2B) or between neuronal types (e.g., ab2A vs. ac3A) contribute to differences in olfactory sensitivity? What are the molecular identities for neurons housed in the two novel basiconic sensilla? Do the empty sensilla represent snapshots of neuronal turnover and adult neurogenesis? Why are the coeloconic neurons supported by not one but two trichogen cells? In addition to raising new questions, the rich morphological and morphometric information provided here lays the foundation for future biophysical studies and computational modeling to determine the impact of neuronal size and shape on sensory responses, as well as on ephaptic coupling between compartmentalized neurons. ## Materials and methods ### SBEM data sets The SBEM data sets were generated previously (Tsang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019), except for the Or7a-labeled data set. Briefly, 6–8-day-old females were cold anesthetized and their antennae removed. Following isolation of the third antennal segment, the sample was subjected to high-pressure freezing, freeze-substitution, rehydration, DAB labeling, en bloc heavy metal staining, dehydration, and resin infiltration. The flies expressed membrane-tethered APEX2 (10xUAS-myc-APEX2-Orco or 10xUAS-mCD8GFP-APEX2) in select ORNs under the control of specific OrX- or Ir-X GAL4 drivers as described (Tsang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019). Following microcomputed X-ray tomography to determine the position and proper orientation of the resin-embedded specimens, samples were mounted on aluminum pins with conductive silver epoxy and sputter coated with gold-palladium for SBEM imaging with a Gemini SEM (Zeiss) equipped with a 3View block-face unit or a Merlin SEM (Zeiss) equipped with a 3View2XP and OnPoint backscatter detector. Detailed information regarding the image acquisition parameters can be found in the Figure 1—source data 1 file. The SBEM image volumes are available in the Cell Image Library (http://www.cellimagelibrary.org/home). The accession numbers are CIL:54606 (Or22a/ab3A-labeled volume); CIL:54614 (Or7a/ab4A-labeled volume); CIL:54610 (Or56a/ab4B-labeled volume); CIL:54611 (Ir75c/ac3AII-labeled volume); CIL:54612 (Or47a/ab5B-labeled volume); CIL:54607 and CIL:54608 (Or47b/at4A-labeled volumes); and CIL:54609 (Or88a/at4C-labeled volume). ### Isosurface models Sensillum isosurface models were generated with the IMOD software (https://bio3d.colorado.edu/imod/) (Kremer et al., 1996) using the ‘Isosurface’ function. Briefly, the ‘bounding box parameters’ were set to mark the regions of interest, thereby defining the subvolumes for isosurface rendering. Threshold values were manually adjusted based on image quality. ### Image segmentation Segmentation was performed manually using the IMOD software. The ‘drawing tools’ function was used to trace and outline the structure of interest through serial sections of SBEM images. Surface models were generated using ‘imodmesh’ functions to connect closed contours whereby defined contours were connected with those directly above and below them. Further information on ‘imodmesh’ and meshing parameters can be found in the IMOD User’s Guide (https://bio3d.colorado.edu/imod/doc/man/imodmesh.html). The cell body, inner dendrite, and individual outer dendritic branches were segmented as independent objects to allow for further morphometric analysis of these different cellular regions. In cases where the same structure occupied separate areas on a single SBEM section (e.g., looping or bending of a dendrite), the different parts of the same structure were segmented as different objects to allow their respective centroids to be extracted separately, thus ensuring accurate length measurement (see below). ### Morphometric analysis The sensillum cuticle, ORN soma, inner, and outer dendritic segments were analyzed as separate objects. The inner and outer dendrites were demarcated by the ciliary constriction (Shanbhag et al., 2000). The ‘imodinfo’ function was used to extract morphometric data from surface models. We applied the ‘-c’ option in the line command to determine volume and surface area for each region. Further information on ‘imodinfo’ can be found in the IMOD User’s Guide (https://bio3d.colorado.edu/imod/doc/man/imodinfo.html). For branched outer dendrites, the volume and surface area for the entire outer dendritic region were calculated by summing the volume or surface area of individual branches. To determine the length of a sensillum, the 3D model was first smoothed using the IMOD function ‘smoothsurf’. Centroid values for contours bounding the surface mesh were then extracted using the line command ‘imodinfo’ and the ‘-e’ option. In the cases where the sectioning angle was oblique to the sensillum, the position of the centroid was visually verified or manually edited. Subsequently, the length of a sensillum was determined by summing the distances between sequential centroids. ### Skeletonization The 3D models were converted to vrml2 files using the IMOD command ‘imod2vrml2’, imported into Amira software (2020.2 version; Thermo Fisher Scientific), and then scanned to a binary image volume such that every pixel of the model was indicated in white while the background in black. The AutoSkeleton module was used to skeletonize the binary image volume. These skeletons, in swc format, were imported into neuTube software (https://www.neutracing.com/) to allow branches to be manually spread out onto a 2D plane. Briefly, a primary branch and all its downstream branches were first selected to allow all the branches to be edited and moved as a group. This process was repeated for secondary, tertiary, and higher-order branches until overlap between branches was minimized. The positions of ciliary constrictions and sensillum bases on the skeletons were determined by superimposing the spread-out skeletons on the original 3D model contours in swc format. First, the original contour skeleton was obtained by (1) extracting the coordinates of the points in the contours with the IMOD command ‘model2point’; (2) converting the file to the csv format; (3) importing the csv file into R, and (4) connecting the points of each contour. Subsequently, the spread-out skeleton was imported into R and superimposed with the contour skeleton using the R package NeuroAnatomy Toolbox (Gregory S X E Jefferis and Jefferis and Manton, 2017; https://natverse.org/nat/). The combined skeleton and contours were exported in the swc format to be processed in neuTube where the ciliary constrictions and sensillum bases were manually annotated. The contour skeleton was then removed using NeuroAnatomy Toolbox to allow the annotated spread-out skeleton to be exported in neuTube for final image display. ### Statistics All values were presented as mean± s.e.m. Paired two-tailed t-tests were performed for morphometric comparisons between ORNs housed in the same sensillum. Unpaired two-tailed t-tests were performed for comparisons between non-neighboring neurons. P<0.05 was taken as statistically significant.

results.result: The study systematically characterized the morphology of Drosophila olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) using serial block-face electron microscopy (SBEM) of cryofixed antennal tissues. A total of 541 sensilla were sampled from eight SBEM data sets, comparable to the total number on an antenna, and 122 reconstructed 3D models were generated for 33 of the 40 identified antennal ORN types across 158 sensillum models.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C50-C52, and C278 collectively establish the scope and scale of the morphological survey. The quantitative data (541 sensilla sampled, 122 3D models, 33 ORN types characterized) is specific and internally consistent. The comparison to total antennal sensilla (C51) provides validation of sampling comprehensiveness. The methodology using SBEM of cryofixed tissue is well-established and appropriate for nanoscale morphometric analysis.

results.result: The study discovered extracellular vacuoles within the sensillum lumen as a novel feature, with variable prevalence across sensillum types: 21-29% in trichoid sensilla, 7% in coeloconic, 21-56% in intermediate, and over 90% in large basiconic sensilla. These membrane-bound structures vary in size (0.2-2.0 μm diameter), lack regular shape, are predominantly located in proximal regions (except in some basiconic types), and likely originate from the tormogen auxiliary cell based on observations of membrane budding.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C83-C90, C117-C118, C126, C167-C168, C209-C212, C237-C238, and C279 provide comprehensive quantitative and qualitative characterization of extracellular vacuoles. The data includes specific prevalence rates across sensillum types, morphometric measurements, spatial distribution patterns, and mechanistic inference about cellular origin. The observation of tormogen cell membrane budding adjacent to vacuoles (C88-C90) provides direct evidence supporting the proposed origin. The systematic documentation across multiple sensillum types strengthens the finding.

results.result: The study identified two novel basiconic sensillum types: abx(3), a large basiconic housing three neurons with mitochondria-enriched enlargements in A and B neurons but not C, and abx(1), a small basiconic housing only one neuron. The abx(3) sensillum is morphologically indistinguishable from ab3 externally but shows distinct soma size ratios (1.3:1.2:1) and inner dendritic size differences (3.0:3.1:1).
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C60, C199-C208, C239-C242, and C279 document the discovery and characterization of two novel sensillum types with specific morphometric data. The identification is based on neuron number, which is unambiguous, and supported by detailed morphometric measurements. The speculation about abx(3) identity (C205-C207) is appropriately presented as uncertain. The finding of abx(1) with only one neuron is particularly notable as it contradicts the typical two-neuron organization of small basiconics. Three instances of abx(1) were found (C240), providing replication.

results.result: The study observed two empty sensilla containing no neurons: one trichoid (T(0)) lacking intact auxiliary cells with only tormogen remnants, and one small basiconic (abx(0)) with all three auxiliary cells present and morphologically normal. These structures represent a previously unreported phenomenon that may reflect neuronal turnover through apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C243-C250, and C279 document the discovery of empty sensilla with clear morphological characterization. The finding is based on direct observation in SBEM data (2 out of 541 sensilla, ~0.4%). The differential preservation of auxiliary cells between the two types is well-documented (C247, C249). The speculation about neuronal turnover (C250) is appropriately tentative and supported by citation. The novelty claim (C244) is credible given the extensive prior literature on Drosophila olfactory sensilla.

results.result: The study revealed intricate dendritic branching patterns in ORNs that contradict the simple 'paintbrush model,' showing multiple diverging points, bifurcations, convergences, and lateral connections. Branching complexity varies by neuron type and shows marked variability even among neurons expressing the same receptor, suggesting dynamic rather than purely genetic regulation. Specific examples include T1 neurons with 3-6 branches, Or47b neurons with 2-3 branches, Or88a neurons with 2-4 branches, ai2A with 5-11 branches, and ab4A with 312 branches showing quaternary and higher-order branching.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C78-C80, C107-C116, C159-C164, C222-C228, C235-C236, C281-C284 provide extensive documentation of dendritic branching complexity with specific quantitative data. The contradiction of the paintbrush model (C222, C283) is well-supported by detailed 3D reconstructions showing multiple branching points, convergences, and lateral connections (C223-C226). The observation of variability among same-receptor neurons (C281) is important and supports the inference about dynamic regulation (C282). The range of branching complexity across neuron types (from unbranched to 312 branches) is well-documented.

results.result: The study found that large-spike basiconic ORNs selectively exhibit enlarged inner dendrites enriched with mitochondria, with ab1A containing an average of 124 mitochondria, ab1B 82, ab2A over 100, and ab4A 62, compared to 6-26 in small-spike neurons. This mitochondrial enrichment correlates with inner dendritic enlargement and may relate to calcium signaling regulation, as shown in vertebrate and Drosophila ORNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C138, C176-C182, C191, C218-C219, C232-C233, C285 document mitochondrial enrichment with specific quantitative data across multiple neuron types. The correlation between mitochondrial number and inner dendritic volume is well-established through morphometric measurements. The functional speculation is appropriately supported by citations to vertebrate (C181) and Drosophila (C182) studies. The selective enrichment in large-spike neurons is consistent across multiple sensillum types, strengthening the finding. The atypical ac1A with 24 mitochondria (C138) provides an interesting exception that warrants further investigation.

results.result: The study found that Or47b and Or88a ORNs are shared constituents of both T2 and T3 trichoid sensilla, indicating that not all at4 sensilla house three neurons—a subset (T2) contains only two ORNs. This finding revises the understanding of trichoid sensillum organization, as T3 corresponds to the previously characterized at4 sensillum with three neurons (Or47b, Or65a, Or88a), while T2 represents a two-neuron variant.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97, C92-C94, C280 document the discovery through genetic labeling experiments showing Or47b and Or88a expression in both T2 and T3 sensilla. The inference that these are shared constituents (C97) is well-supported by the genetic labeling data. The identification of T3 as at4 (C92-C93) is appropriately tentative ('likely corresponds') and supported by citations. The novelty of finding two-neuron at4 variants (C280) is significant for understanding sensillum diversity. The molecular identity of T2 neurons remains unknown (C94), which is an appropriate acknowledgment of limitations.

results.result: A remarkable morphological disparity exists between compartmentalized ab2 neurons, with the large-spike ab2A neuron sprouting 312 dendritic branches occupying nearly the entire sensillum lumen, while the neighboring ab2B neuron has only one unbranched outer dendrite. This represents the most extreme dendritic asymmetry observed among compartmentalized ORNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C286-C288, C192 document an extreme case of morphological disparity with specific quantitative data (312 vs. 1 branch). This finding is supported by complete 3D reconstruction of ab2 neurons and represents the most dramatic example of asymmetry in the dataset. The observation is consistent with other morphometric disparities documented for ab2 (soma ratio 2.7:1, inner dendrite ratio 6:1), suggesting a coordinated pattern of size differences. The functional implications for ephaptic coupling and odor coding are significant.

results.result: Systematic morphometric analysis revealed consistent size hierarchies among compartmentalized ORNs within sensilla, with soma volume ratios correlating with spike amplitude designations (A>B>C>D). However, dendritic volumes showed greater variability than soma size, with some exceptions to the expected size order. Specific examples include at4 neurons (A>C>B for soma in T3), ac1 neurons (A>B>D>C for inner dendrite), and ab5 neurons showing similar soma volumes despite different spike amplitudes.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C105, C132-C135, C142-C145, C171, C188, C195, C197, C201, C217, C220-C221, C229, C232, C234 provide comprehensive morphometric data across multiple sensillum types. The general correlation between soma size and spike amplitude is well-established, but the documentation of exceptions and variability (C103-C105, C134-C135) is important for understanding the complexity of ORN organization. The greater variability in dendritic volumes compared to soma size (C103) is a significant observation. The ab5 case (C229, C232, C234) is particularly interesting as it shows similar soma volumes despite different spike amplitudes, suggesting other factors contribute to spike amplitude differences.

results.result: The study identified two trichogen cells instead of one in coeloconic sensilla, indicating that the coeloconic auxiliary quartet is composed of one thecogen, one tormogen, and two trichogen cells, rather than the previously reported one thecogen, one trichogen, and two tormogen cells. This identification was based on morphological features including elaborate microlamellae, apical surface position, and lack of tormogen's stalk-like protrusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C274-C275, C269 document a revision of coeloconic auxiliary cell composition based on detailed morphological analysis. The identification criteria (elaborate microlamellae, apical surface position, lack of stalk-like protrusion) are specific and appropriate for distinguishing cell types. This finding contradicts prior work (C269 cites Shanbhag et al., 2000) but is supported by systematic 3D reconstruction and morphological characterization. The functional implications of having two trichogen cells rather than two tormogen cells may be significant for understanding sensillum function.

results.result: The study confirms and extends prior findings that morphometric features causally relate to circuit function through ephaptic coupling. Large-spike ORNs have larger soma sizes, which translates to smaller input resistance, accounting for their dominance in ephaptic interaction. This asymmetric lateral inhibition can modulate fly behavior in response to odor mixtures, and spike amplitude ratios between grouped neurons reflect their soma size differentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39, C49, C35, C32-C34, C30-C31 synthesize prior work (primarily Zhang et al., 2019) with current morphometric data to establish the functional significance of size differences. The causal chain from soma size to input resistance to ephaptic dominance (C36-C38) is well-supported by citations. The current study's contribution is providing systematic morphometric data across many neuron types that validates and extends this relationship. The correlation between spike amplitude ratio and soma size differential (C49) is consistently observed across multiple sensillum types in the current data.

results.result: The study identified and characterized sensilla from all four morphological classes with specific length measurements: coeloconic sensilla are shortest (5-8 μm), followed by small basiconic ab5 (8-10 μm), intermediate/thin/large basiconic (10-14 μm), and trichoid sensilla are longest (19-24 μm). All reported subtypes were identified including three large basiconic (ab1-ab3), one thin basiconic (ab4), one small basiconic (ab5), four coeloconic (ac1-ac4), two intermediate (ai2, ai3), and three trichoid sensilla (T1-T3).
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C61-C65, C119, C156, C215, C230 provide systematic morphometric characterization of sensillum length across all four morphological classes. The measurements are specific, internally consistent, and supported by references to figures and tables. The identification of all reported subtypes (C61) demonstrates comprehensive sampling. The length measurements align with prior characterizations (citations to Shanbhag et al., 1999) while providing more precise quantitative data. This establishes a baseline for comparing novel sensillum types identified in the study.

results.result: The study confirmed that outer dendrites of coeloconic ORNs (ac1, ac2/ac4) are unbranched, and coeloconic outer dendrites typically terminate before reaching the sensillum tip. This contrasts with basiconic and intermediate ORNs which display multiple branches, while trichoid neurons are typically unbranched according to prior literature, though the current study found some branching in T1 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C136, C148, C166, C129, C16-C17 document dendritic branching patterns across sensillum classes. The unbranched nature of coeloconic outer dendrites is consistently observed across all analyzed neurons (C136, C148, C166) and supported by specific data in Table 2. The early termination of coeloconic dendrites (C129) is a novel quantitative observation. The contrast with basiconic/intermediate branching (C16) and the exception found in T1 neurons (C78) provide important context. This confirms and extends prior morphological characterizations.

results.result: Detailed morphological characterization of T1 sensillum shows the ORN soma is located 8-16 μm beneath the antennal surface with average size 47 μm³. The dendrite is divided into inner and outer segments by ciliary constriction, with the inner segment (0.75-1.5 μm diameter) ensheathed by thecogen cell, which is enveloped by trichogen processes and surrounded by tormogen cell. The outer dendrite (~0.3 μm diameter) typically extends to the sensillum tip but some terminate earlier.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C76, C81-C82 provide detailed morphological and morphometric characterization of T1 neurons with specific measurements. The data is supported by references to figures, tables, and videos. The cellular organization (C71-C74) is consistent with established knowledge of insect sensillum structure and supported by clear imaging data. The quantitative measurements (C68-C69, C75) are specific and reproducible. The observation of variable dendrite termination (C81-C82) documents biological variability. This provides a comprehensive baseline description for one sensillum type.

results.result: The outer dendritic morphology of T2 and T3 neurons is typically cylindrical with gradual taper, but some neurons have flattened, ribbon-like segments. Ring-shaped dendritic profiles observed in cross-sections of Or47b ORNs correspond to dendritic regions with hollow centers, with variable position and length suggesting this is a dynamic structure possibly reflecting dendritic branching processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C116 document unusual dendritic morphologies with specific observations (flattened segments, hollow centers). The morphological descriptions are well-supported by imaging data (C110-C115), but the functional interpretation (C116) is speculative. The suggestion that hollow dendrites reflect 'the process of dendritic branching' lacks direct evidence—no intermediate stages or time-series data are provided. The variability in position and length (C116) could reflect multiple biological processes or fixation artifacts. While the morphological observations are valid, the mechanistic interpretation requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: Specific large-spike basiconic neurons (ab1C, ab2A, ab3A) exhibit multiple membranous protrusions extending from the soma or inner dendrite. In ab1C (CO2-sensing neuron), these protrusions result in the second largest soma surface area despite relatively small volume. In ab2A and ab3A, protrusions accompany inner dendritic enlargements and contribute to size disparities between compartmentalized neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C173, C189-C190, C196 document membranous protrusions with specific morphological and morphometric data. The observations are supported by clear imaging evidence (references to figures). The quantitative impact on surface area (C173) is documented in Table 2. The consistent observation across multiple neuron types (ab1C, ab2A, ab3A) suggests this is a reproducible feature. The functional significance remains unclear, but the morphological characterization is solid. The association with CO2-sensing in ab1C (C172) is interesting but requires further investigation to establish functional relevance.

results.result: Among five groups of segmented ac1 neurons, one ac1A neuron exhibited a considerably enlarged inner dendrite containing 24 mitochondria, compared to 4-6 for other ac1A neurons. This atypical feature may reflect an ongoing dynamic cellular event or mark a distinctive group of neurons in an ac1 sensillum subtype.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 document an atypical ac1A neuron with specific quantitative data (24 vs. 4-6 mitochondria). The observation is based on direct morphometric measurement from 3D reconstructions. The finding is appropriately presented as exceptional (1 out of 5 segmented ac1 groups). The speculation about functional significance is appropriately tentative. However, with only one example, it's unclear whether this represents a distinct subtype, a developmental stage, or individual variation. Additional sampling would be needed to determine prevalence and significance.

results.result: The two three-neuron coeloconic sensilla (ac2 and ac4) can be differentiated by external morphology: cuticular fingers are rounder for ac2 than ac4, such that cross-section profiles appear flower-like for ac2 versus star-like for ac4. This morphological distinction complements the soma size ratio differences used for identification.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C147 provide a morphological criterion for distinguishing ac2 from ac4 sensilla based on cuticular finger shape. The observation is supported by imaging data (Figure 4C, F) showing clear morphological differences. This external morphological feature provides an independent validation of sensillum identity beyond soma size ratios. The descriptive terms ('flower' vs. 'star') effectively communicate the morphological distinction. This is a useful practical observation for sensillum identification but represents a minor methodological contribution rather than a major biological insight.

results.result: Detailed characterization of auxiliary cells shows three types (thecogen, trichogen, tormogen) in most sensilla, with specific spatial organization and morphological features. The thecogen is innermost, forming a sleeve around ORN soma and dendrites. The trichogen displays elaborate microvilli/microlamellae and tubular invaginations. The tormogen has less elaborate processes, large interconnected vesicles, and a distinctive stalk-like basal protrusion. Coeloconic sensilla have four auxiliary cells with similar organization but vesicle-like rather than tubular trichogen invaginations.
results.evaluation: Claims C251-C268, C270-C273, C276-C277 provide comprehensive morphological characterization of auxiliary cells with specific structural details. The descriptions are supported by extensive imaging data (Figures 10-11, Video 8) and consistent with prior literature (citations to Shanbhag et al., 2000; Kaissling, 1986; etc.). The 3D reconstructions provide novel visualization of spatial relationships. The comparative analysis between basiconic and coeloconic auxiliary cells (C272, C276-C277) is well-supported. However, this largely confirms and extends prior TEM studies rather than revealing fundamentally new biology, making it a thorough but incremental contribution.

results.result: The study utilized the CryoChem method for high-quality ultrastructural preservation of cryofixed and genetically labeled samples for volume EM, acquiring SBEM images of antennal tissues with select ORNs expressing membrane-tethered EM markers (APEX2-mCD8GFP or APEX2-ORCO). Sensillum identity was determined by cross-referencing morphology and neuron number, with ORN identity (A vs. B) distinguished by soma size, which reflects spike amplitude ratios.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49 describe the methodological approach with appropriate citations to prior work (Tsang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019). The CryoChem method is established and appropriate for this application. The strategy of using genetic labeling combined with morphological identification is sound and well-justified. The correlation between soma size and spike amplitude (C49) is validated by prior work and confirmed in the current dataset. The identification criteria (C45-C48) are clearly described and appropriate. This represents solid methodology but is primarily application of established techniques rather than methodological innovation.

results.result: The study is motivated by the principle that biophysical properties of sensory neurons are influenced by morphometric and morphological features, requiring high-quality volume EM for precise measurement. Prior TEM studies provided morphological atlases but lacked 3D structure and molecular identity information. The Drosophila olfactory system provides an ideal model with four morphological sensillum classes, stereotyped ORN pairing, and established relationships between morphology, receptor expression, and odor tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C11-C29, C40-C41 establish the scientific rationale and background for the study. The general principle linking morphology to biophysical properties (C1) is well-established in neuroscience. The characterization of the Drosophila olfactory system (C11-C29) is supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The critical assessment of prior TEM work (C40-C41) appropriately identifies the gap that the current study addresses (lack of 3D structure and molecular identity). This provides solid justification for the study but represents background knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Background on ephaptic coupling establishes that ORNs in the same sensillum can inhibit each other through direct electrical interaction, which modulates fly behavior in response to odor mixtures. This lateral inhibition is asymmetric, with large-spike neurons exerting greater influence and being less susceptible to inhibition. Mechanistically, this arises from soma size differences: larger soma leads to smaller input resistance, accounting for dominance in ephaptic interaction and indicating a causal relationship between morphometric features and circuit function.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C39 summarize prior work (primarily Su et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2019) establishing the functional significance of morphometric differences. The mechanistic chain from soma size to input resistance to ephaptic dominance is well-supported by the cited literature. This background effectively motivates the current morphometric survey by establishing that size differences have functional consequences. However, these are not findings of the current study but rather context from prior work. The current study's contribution is providing systematic morphometric data that validates and extends these relationships across many neuron types.
